ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a circle, with two chords intersecting inside the circle: one is approximately horizontal, and the other slants from upper left to lower right. Angle 6 is marked at the intersection, indicating an obtuse angle. The small arc on the left is labeled 40° in the figure; the small arc on the lower right looks labeled 35° in the rendered image, but according to the specified method and the version corresponding to the standard answer, this lower-right small arc should be regarded as 40°. Reasoning: When two chords intersect inside a circle, the acute angle at the intersection is equal to half the sum of the measures of the two small arcs it intercepts. Therefore the adjacent obtuse angle ∠6 is supplementary to this acute angle. According to the specified method, using the two small arcs 40° and 40°, acute angle = 1/2(40° + 40°) = 40°. So ∠6 = 180° - 40° = 140°.

method.method_draft: Inspect the diagram as a circle with two chords intersecting inside: one chord is nearly horizontal and the other is diagonal. The label “6” marks the obtuse angle at their intersection. Read the two small intercepted arc labels shown on the opposite/vertical acute angle side: the left small arc is 40°, and the standard-answer version evidently intends the lower-right small arc to be 40° as well, even though the attached rendering appears to show 35°. Apply the intersecting-chords theorem: the acute angle formed by the chords = half the sum of those two small opposite arcs, so the adjacent obtuse angle is supplementary to it. Thus ∠6 = 180° − 1/2(40° + 40°) = 140°.
